newsitem.title: GERMANY: D.Telekom "smart" mobile phone under fire.
newsitem.headline: D.Telekom "smart" mobile phone under fire.

text.p: Deutsche Telekom AG, the German telecommunications group, plans to launch a new mobile phone service next month that works like a pre-paid phone card and has competitors up in arms even before it appears.

According to company documents obtained by Reuters, under the new "Telly-D1 Xtra" service customers will be able to charge their phones like a battery with a fixed volume of calls instead of using the current pay-as-you go method. They would no longer have to pay a monthly basic charge.

Deutsche Telekom declined to comment on the new service, its latest effort to shake up the fiercely competitive mobile phone market with new inexpensive rates and services, but said details would be released at a news conference on Thursday.

The service is largely aimed at winning back market share from mobile resellers -- company's such as Daimler-Benz AG's Debitel GmbH, which sells subscriptions to leading mobile phone services but itself has no network.

The Association of Mobile Service Providers (VAM) lobby group has already asked the government to block the service, complaining that the way Telekom plans to market it violates the terms of its D1 operating licence.

"The service providers see this as an obvious effort to force them out of the targeted market segment," said VAM managing director Gerd Eickers in a letter to the post and telecommunications ministry that was obtained by Reuters.
Eickers wrote that the new system that Telekom plans to install for the service would make it impossible for resellers to provide comparable services at similar rates.
Resellers would also be restricted to selling the service as an agent of D1, rather than as independent providers.
"The members of our association see this treatment as a violation of the terms of the D1 licence," Eickers said.
The post and telecommunications ministry declined to comment on the letter.
The new Telly-D1 Xtra service would carry high per minute charges -- 1.99 marks during the day and 99 pfennigs at night -- but this would be offset by not having monthly charges.
The novelty of the service, however, is the fact that customers will know in advance how much they will pay each month for use of the mobile phone.

The Telekom documents identified potential customers such as parents who want children to be reachable by mobile phone but still want to keep phone bills under control or companies that want additional phones for employees without risking high phone bills.

The new service would be offered in a package with a one-off charge of 249 marks, which includes the initial connection fee, a mobile telephone from Siemens AG, and the first month's calling balance of 50 marks.

Customers would then call Telekom once a month to have the smart card in the phone "charged" like a rechargable battery to the sum of 50 marks or raise this limit by 30, 60 or 90 marks to a maximum of 350 marks per month.
Up to 350 marks could be transferred to the next months and callers would be alerted automatically when the smart card volume fell to 10 marks.
Subscribers to the new service would not be able to use the phones outside of Germany because of billing restrictions.
